findings.rule: METHODS §6.3 rate the claim as worded; brief checks A and E
findings.issue: The statement leads with the unadjusted, highly heterogeneous estimates (I² 80% and 90%) although the grade reasoning says the claim rests on the adjusted estimate. It also leaves out that most pooled studies were cross-sectional and drawn from treatment, psychiatric, emergency or criminal-justice samples, so the order of use and psychosis is unknown; that the symptoms-versus-disorder contrast is a post hoc subgroup; and that for any use the association with a diagnosed disorder was not statistically clear. 'Half of the studies' should be 'populations' (8 populations from 20 papers).
findings.evidence: sc_mcketin_2019 key_findings[0] (47 of 59 pooled studies cross-sectional), sample.recruitment and selection_effects (most comparisons within substance-using, clinical and custodial samples), analysis.preregistration_detail (subgroups post hoc), key_findings[5] (any use, diagnosed disorder 1.3, 1.0–1.9, p=0.087), exposure.polysubstance (authors: unadjusted estimates likely inflated); evidence[0]–[2]; evidence[5] (4 of 8 populations).
findings.proposed: In observational studies, mostly cross-sectional (47 of 59 pooled studies) and mostly in treatment, psychiatric, emergency or criminal-justice samples in which the comparison group often also used other drugs, people with an amphetamine use disorder (amphetamine or methamphetamine) had higher odds of psychosis than people without one: odds ratio 2.4 (95% CI 1.6–3.5; 4 studies, I² 35%) in studies that adjusted for some combination of demographics, other substance use and premorbid risk. Unadjusted estimates, which the review's authors consider inflated by co-occurring risk factors, were 3.0 (1.9–4.8; 13 studies, I² 90%) for use disorder and 2.0 (1.3–3.3; 7 studies, I² 80%) for any use. In post hoc subgroups the association was stronger for psychotic symptoms than for diagnosed psychotic disorders; for any use, the association with a diagnosed disorder was not statistically clear (1.3, 1.0–1.9). Most studies cannot show whether use preceded psychosis. No threshold level of use could be estimated; more frequent use went with more psychotic symptoms in 4 of the 8 study populations that examined it.

findings.rule: brief check B; METHODS §9
findings.issue: 'A lasting psychotic illness' is not what the review measured: 'diagnosed psychotic disorder' includes substance-induced disorders and says nothing about duration. 'Roughly two to three times the odds..., more for people with a use disorder' double counts (the use-disorder figures are the two-to-three range). The plain also drops that the studies were mostly of people in treatment, hospital or prison and could not show which came first. Because cl_meth_psychosis_dose's replacement in the at-a-glance box is likely to be this claim (see monograph finding), its plain text will be shown there.
findings.evidence: evidence[2] (symptoms vs diagnosed disorder); sc_mcketin_2019 outcomes.instruments (diagnoses include clinical, hospital and registry diagnoses), key_findings[0] and sample.selection_effects.
findings.proposed: In studies mostly of people in drug treatment, hospitals or prisons, people with a meth or amphetamine use disorder were more likely to have psychotic symptoms such as paranoia or hallucinations than people without one: about two and a half times the odds after taking some other differences into account. Studies of any use found about twice the odds, without that adjustment. The link was clearer for symptoms than for a diagnosed psychotic illness. Most studies measured use and symptoms at the same time, so they cannot show which came first, and they could not say how much use it takes for the risk to rise.

findings.rule: GRADE; METHODS §6.3 (rate as worded; risk-of-bias rule)
findings.issue: The reasoning justifies no risk-of-bias downgrade by the consistency of the adjusted estimate (I² 35%), which is an inconsistency argument, not a risk-of-bias one, and says the claim rests on the adjusted estimate while the current statement headlines the unadjusted ones (unadjusted comparisons with known confounders are a §6.3 reason to downgrade). It does not mention that publication bias was not assessed (AMSTAR 2 critically low). If the statement keeps the unadjusted estimates as its headline, risk of bias should be downgraded one level (certainty very low).
findings.evidence: sc_mcketin_2019 risk_of_bias (overall critically low; item 15 'no'), comparison.controls_other_drug_use (comparison groups mostly used other drugs; authors say this biases toward the null), comparison.unmeasured_premorbid; evidence[4].
findings.proposed: With the statement restructured as proposed (certainty unchanged, low): 'Observational, mostly cross-sectional; starts low. The claim is an association and rests on the adjusted use-disorder estimate (2.4, 1.6–3.5; 4 studies, I² 35%); the unadjusted estimates are context, labelled as likely inflated. Risk of bias not downgraded: the adjusted studies accounted for some combination of demographics, other substance use and premorbid risk, and comparison groups mostly also used other drugs, which the authors argue biases toward the null; residual confounding by unmeasured premorbid factors (family history of psychosis, childhood trauma) remains and is why the claim is worded as an association. Inconsistency not downgraded for the adjusted estimate; the unadjusted ones are heterogeneous (I² 80–90%). Publication bias was not assessed by the review (AMSTAR 2 critically low); not downgraded, noted. Not upgraded for dose–response: frequency was associated in 4 of 8 populations. McKetin et al. (2013), rated separately as cl_meth_psychosis_dose, is inside the pooled estimates, so the two claims are not independent evidence.'

findings.rule: brief check A (statement content without an anchor); METHODS §6.2
findings.issue: Three parts of the statement have no anchor: that the comparison group usually also used other drugs (added by the second reader), which covariate families lie behind the adjusted estimates, and the design mix of the pooled studies.
findings.evidence: sc_mcketin_2019 sample.recruitment ('Results › Characteristics of included studies'), key_findings[0], analysis.covariates, exposure.polysubstance.

findings.rule: METHODS §6.3 overlapping evidence; internal consistency
findings.issue: The card says 'Callaghan 2012' is inside the pooled estimates, but the encyclopedia's callaghan_2012 is the Parkinson's-disease study, which cannot be in a meta-analysis of psychosis, violence, suicidality, depression and anxiety. The Callaghan study meant is presumably the California record-linkage cohort of methamphetamine use and later schizophrenia (Am J Psychiatry 2012), which the Bramness card cites and which is not on the reading list, although it bears directly on cl_meth_psychosis_course.
findings.evidence: sc_mcketin_2019 replication.where_it_stands; sc_bramness_2012 replication.timeline (2012, California record-linkage cohort on later schizophrenia); data/references callaghan_2012 (Parkinson's disease, Drug Alcohol Depend 2012).
findings.proposed: Change the card text to: 'Primary studies central to the encyclopedia are inside the pooled estimates (McKetin et al., 2013; and, by its outcome, the California schizophrenia cohort of Callaghan et al., 2012, Am J Psychiatry, not the Parkinson's-disease study held as callaghan_2012), so claims must not cite them as independent support.' Add the Am J Psychiatry cohort to the methamphetamine DOI list.

findings.rule: METHODS §6.3 large effect; GRADE (rating up evidence with serious limitations)
findings.issue: The large-effect upgrade breaks §6.3: under the most adjusted model the estimates are 2.25 (1.29–3.90) and 3.90 (1.80–8.45); symptoms were present in 25% of person-months, so odds ratios overstate risk ratios; and a remaining bias can run away from the null (symptoms rated by the interviewer who had just recorded that month's use). The reasoning also omits the card's 'high' ROBINS-E domain (selection), and two upgrades sit on evidence downgraded for risk of bias, which GRADE generally reserves for evidence without serious limitations. The encyclopedia's own Arunogiri card criticizes that review's 'moderate' for frequency of use for upgrading this same single study for effect size and gradient. The claim is in the at-a-glance 'best established' box only because of these upgrades.
findings.evidence: sc_mcketin_2013 risk_of_bias (overall high; selection high; outcome measurement some concerns), key_findings[2] (273 of 1064 months), key_findings[8] (2.25 and 3.90), reporting_issues[0] (number contributing to fixed effects unreported) and [4] (non-blind rating); sc_arunogiri_2018 interpretation_gap.claimed; evidence[4]–[5].
findings.proposed: large_effect 0; dose_response 1; risk_of_bias 1; certainty 'low' (low −1 +1). Reasoning: 'Prospective within-person cohort; starts low. Comparing each person with themselves removes stable confounders, the main weakness of the cross-sectional literature. Risk of bias −1 (ROBINS-E overall high): selection (278 of 501 analysed; 138 excluded for missing follow-up interviews; the number contributing to the fixed-effects estimates is not reported), self-reported use, and symptoms rated by the interviewer who recorded that month's use. Dose–response +1: within the same people the odds rose from 4.0 (1–15 days) to 11.2 (16 or more days), and the gradient persisted under the most adjusted model (2.25 to 3.90); kept because the within-person design addresses the main reason observational evidence starts low, although GRADE generally reserves upgrading for evidence without serious limitations (a strict reading gives very low). Not upgraded for large effect: under the most adjusted model the estimates are 2.25 (1.29–3.90) and 3.90 (1.80–8.45); symptoms were present in 25% of person-months, so odds ratios overstate risk ratios; unblinded rating could bias away from the null; and this is one cohort.'

findings.rule: brief check B (dropped qualifiers 'predicted' and 'in months without heavy cannabis or alcohol use')
findings.issue: The plain presents the 7% and about-half figures as observed frequencies; they are model predictions for months without heavy cannabis or alcohol use. It also drops that most participants injected, that disability was among the added factors (which may be consequences of use), and that use and symptoms were measured over the same month.
findings.evidence: evidence[3] (predicted risks, fewer than 16 days of cannabis or alcohol use); evidence[4]; sc_mcketin_2013 sample.demographics (83% had injected), exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route (injecting in 79% of months of use), cannot_establish (direction within a month).
findings.proposed: In about 280 people dependent on meth in Australia, most of whom injected it, each person was compared with themselves at four points over three years. The study's model predicted psychotic symptoms such as paranoia or hallucinations in about 7% of months without meth and in about half of months with meth on 16 or more days (in both cases for months without heavy cannabis or alcohol use). The link was smaller, but still there, after also accounting for unemployment, housing, income, distress and disability at the time, which may themselves be results of use. Because use and symptoms were measured over the same month, the study cannot show which came first.

findings.rule: brief check E (reverse causation; route); METHODS §9 (population, route and pattern)
findings.issue: 'Followed for up to 3 years' hides that use and symptoms were measured over the same one-month windows (four windows), so which came first within a month is unknown, and the statement omits the route (injecting in 79% of months of use), which limits generalization to people who smoke or snort methamphetamine.
findings.evidence: sc_mcketin_2013 design_detail, cannot_establish, key_findings[3] (612 of 1064 months with use; median 8 days; injecting the main route in 79%); evidence[6] (authors limit findings to dependence).
findings.proposed: Replace 'followed for up to 3 years' with 'assessed in four one-month windows over 3 years (injecting was the main route in 79% of months of use)', and end the statement with: 'Use and symptoms were measured over the same month, so the study cannot show which came first; the authors limit the findings to people with methamphetamine dependence.' Add an anchor: mcketin_2013, 'Results › Characteristics of the sample, 2nd paragraph; Table', extracted 'Methamphetamine used in 612 of 1064 months (median 8 days); injecting the main route in 79% of those months.'

findings.rule: METHODS §5.3 (narrative reviews are never primary evidence); §1.4 principle 3
findings.issue: Every number in the claim is a second-hand figure from three narrative reviews, and each of their cards says these frequency, duration and transition figures must be taken from the primary sources before use. A systematic review of the symptom profile and course of methamphetamine psychosis (Voce et al., 2019, DOI list item 50) and the primary Thai cohort are on the reading list but unread.
findings.evidence: sc_glasner_edwards_2014 risk_of_bias.reasoning and replication.where_it_stands (figures need primary-study cards), reporting_issues[4] (Thai cohort: Kittirattanapaiboon et al., 2010); sc_wearne_2018 risk_of_bias.reasoning; sc_bramness_2012 risk_of_bias.reasoning; search-logs/methamphetamine_DOI-LIST.md item 50.
findings.proposed: Rebuild the claim on Voce et al. (2019) and the primary cohorts: the Thai cohort (Kittirattanapaiboon et al., 2010), the two Taiwanese 1- and 3-month studies (refs 12 and 47 of Glasner-Edwards & Mooney, 2014) and the California record-linkage cohort of later schizophrenia (Callaghan et al., 2012, Am J Psychiatry). Until then set verification.status to 'draft', keep the claim out of the at-a-glance box, and end the statement with: 'These figures have not yet been checked in the primary studies.'

findings.rule: brief check E (premorbid vulnerability, selection); METHODS §9 language
findings.issue: 'A substantial share' is an evaluative phrase for a range from 5% to about 39%. The statement does not say that a later schizophrenia diagnosis cannot show whether methamphetamine caused a lasting illness, revealed an existing vulnerability, or whether the first episode was a primary psychosis attributed to drug use, which is the central question of the Bramness review. The 16% and 17% come from two Taiwanese studies from one group, in people without earlier episodes or a family history of schizophrenia.
findings.evidence: sc_bramness_2012 can_establish and key_findings[8]–[9] (vulnerability model); sc_glasner_edwards_2014 key_findings[7] (Taiwanese; no earlier episodes or family history) and interpretation_gap.results_show; evidence[0], [3], [5].
findings.proposed: Second-hand figures in narrative reviews, mostly from hospital samples, suggest that most methamphetamine-associated psychotic episodes resolve within days to a month of stopping use but that a minority persist: 16% and 17% were still psychotic after 1 and 3 months of abstinence in two small Taiwanese studies from one research group (people without earlier episodes or a family history of schizophrenia), and 10–28% beyond 6 months in hospital series. Between 5% (China) and about 39% (a Thai cohort of more than 1,000 people first hospitalized, within 5–6 years) later received a schizophrenia diagnosis, and 19–30% in register studies of amphetamine-induced psychosis. These figures cannot show whether methamphetamine caused a lasting illness, revealed an existing vulnerability, or whether some first episodes were primary psychoses attributed to drug use. Recurrence with renewed use is common in clinical series, and Japanese series describe recurrences after stress without renewed use.

findings.rule: brief check A; internal consistency (changelog vs anchors)
findings.issue: The sentence on recurrences triggered by stress without renewed use has no anchor. The changelog attributes it to Bramness et al. (2012), but the only Bramness anchor concerns later primary psychosis; the Glasner-Edwards anchor lists stress among triggers but not recurrence without renewed use.
findings.evidence: sc_bramness_2012 key_findings[4] ('Prevalence and clinical presentation, 4th paragraph': Japanese series, psychosis lasting years, stress-triggered spontaneous relapses after remission); changelog v0.2.1; evidence[1], [4].

findings.rule: brief check B; display in the research-gaps list and (if adopted) the at-a-glance box
findings.issue: The plain opens with a finding ('Most meth-related psychosis clears within days to weeks') that the research-gaps section lists as if established, and it does not say that a later schizophrenia diagnosis does not show that methamphetamine caused it.
findings.evidence: site/src/app.views.js gapsHtml (shows the first sentence of each very-low plain); statement; sc_bramness_2012 key_findings[9].
findings.proposed: How long does meth-related psychosis last, and how often does it turn into a long-term illness? Not known with any precision. Reviews quoting mostly hospital studies say most episodes clear within days to a month of stopping and a minority last months, and that between about 1 in 20 and 2 in 5 people were later diagnosed with schizophrenia. That does not show meth caused the later illness: some people may have been vulnerable already. Psychosis often comes back with renewed use.

findings.rule: METHODS §5.3 (narrative reviews never primary evidence)
findings.issue: The claim rests only on Wearne & Cornish (2018, classified on its card as a narrative review, critically low) and Bramness et al. (2012); the Wearne card says each primary study needs its own card before it supports a claim. A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of positive and negative symptoms in methamphetamine-induced psychosis versus schizophrenia (Cohen-Laroque et al., DOI list item 52) is on the reading list but unread.

findings.proposed: Rebuild on Cohen-Laroque et al. (2024) and the primary studies that carry the key contrasts (Chen et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2016; McKetin et al., 2017; Srisurapanont et al., 2011). Until then set verification.status to 'draft', keep the claim out of any summary box, and say in the statement that the evidence is a narrative review of 12 small studies (text below).

findings.rule: METHODS §6.3 (absence of evidence); brief checks A and E
findings.issue: 'Positive-symptom severity was mostly similar' and 'Symptoms alone do not reliably separate the two' turn non-significant differences in small samples (as few as 9 in a group; the review notes small samples may make the disorders look alike) and an author's judgment that separation is probably very difficult into findings. 'Visual and tactile hallucinations may be more frequent' was shown directly only in one study of persistent psychosis (Wang et al., 2016), and the review's table and text disagree for another. The persistent-versus-acute contrast (Chen et al., 2015) assessed the acute group about 9 weeks after its episode, when its symptoms may already have resolved.
findings.evidence: sc_wearne_2018 analysis.power, interpretation_gap.results_show, key_findings[4] (acute group assessed about 9 weeks later), [5], [6], reporting_issues[0]; sc_bramness_2012 key_findings[3]; evidence[1]–[5].
findings.proposed: A narrative review of 12 small studies directly comparing methamphetamine psychosis with schizophrenia (1990–2017; printed sample sizes 22–285, some compared groups as small as 9 vs 33) found no significant difference in positive-symptom severity in most comparisons, though samples this small could miss real differences; negative symptoms were milder in methamphetamine psychosis in the four studies that examined them in detail (one other found no difference). More visual and tactile hallucinations were shown directly in one study of persistent methamphetamine psychosis (about 53 per group). In one study (Chen et al., 2015), psychosis persisting more than a month into abstinence did not differ significantly from schizophrenia on BPRS total and positive scores, while the acute group, assessed about 9 weeks after its episode, scored lower. No study has tested whether symptoms can tell the two apart in an individual; reviewers judge it difficult.

findings.rule: METHODS §6.3 (no-detectable-difference wording needs precision)
findings.issue: 'Equal to schizophrenia' claims equivalence from a non-significant difference between groups of 56 and 54, and the magnitude omits that the review gives no effect sizes, that it names different instruments for the same study, and that the acute comparison group was assessed about 9 weeks after its episode.
findings.evidence: sc_wearne_2018 analysis.effect_sizes (directions and significance only), key_findings[4], reporting_issues[3] (Chen et al.: PANSS in one passage, BPRS in Table 1); evidence[2].
findings.proposed: No effect sizes reported (direction and significance only). Positive symptoms: no significant difference in most acute comparisons (PANSS, BPRS; groups as small as 9 vs 33). Negative symptoms: milder in methamphetamine psychosis in four detailed comparisons. Persistent methamphetamine psychosis (n=56) did not differ significantly from schizophrenia (n=54) on BPRS total and positive scores; the acute group (n=50) was assessed about 9 weeks after its episode (Chen et al., 2015, as reviewed; the review names BPRS in Table 1 and PANSS in one passage).

findings.rule: brief check B; METHODS §6.3
findings.issue: 'Hallucinations and paranoid beliefs are similarly severe' drops 'in most small comparisons' and states similarity as a finding; 'may involve more seeing or feeling things' does not say this came from one study; 'can't reliably tell them apart' states as shown what has not been tested.
findings.evidence: As for the statement finding above.
findings.proposed: Meth psychosis and schizophrenia can look alike. In small studies, hallucinations and paranoid beliefs were not clearly different in severity, but studies this small can miss differences. People with meth psychosis tended to have fewer 'negative' symptoms (flatness, withdrawal), and one study found more seeing or feeling things that aren't there. Psychosis still present a month after stopping looked more like schizophrenia. No study has tested whether symptoms can tell them apart in one person.

findings.rule: internal consistency (outcome field vs statement)
findings.issue: The outcome field lists cognitive symptoms, but the statement says nothing about cognition.
findings.evidence: Claim outcome field; sc_wearne_2018 interpretation_gap.results_show (Chen et al., 2015: persistent psychosis like schizophrenia on cognitive tests, acute like non-psychotic users; acute-sample studies found no difference except on one attention test in one study of 30 vs 30).
findings.proposed: Change the outcome to 'Positive and negative symptoms', or add to the statement: 'On cognitive tests, persistent methamphetamine psychosis performed like schizophrenia and acute psychosis like non-psychotic users in one study; studies of acute psychosis found no difference except on one attention test in one study of 30 vs 30.'

findings.rule: brief check A (every number in an anchor)
findings.issue: 'Amphetamine use disorder was not significantly associated with major depression (OR 1.2, 0.5–2.7)': these numbers appear in no anchor of this claim. The card gives the estimate as unadjusted, for 'depression' (6 studies, I² 87%), and says the null came from samples with high levels of other substance use or clinical conditions; 'major depression' is not supported by the card.
findings.evidence: sc_mcketin_2019 key_findings[3] (Table 2, lower panel: depression 1.2, 0.5–2.7, 6 studies, I² 87%, not significant) and key_findings[8] (null came from samples with high other substance use or clinical conditions).

findings.rule: brief check A (selective use of a cited source); METHODS §9 (population as studied)
findings.issue: The statement reports the 2019 review's null use-disorder estimate but omits the 2023 update's use-disorder estimates from a source the claim cites (unadjusted 3.46, 2.04–5.89, 2 cross-sectional studies; adjusted 2.80 from a single twin study whose drug class must be checked); the two reviews differ because the update excluded comparisons with people who use other drugs. The opening says 'Methamphetamine use' although both reviews pool methamphetamine with amphetamine (one longitudinal cohort measured 'speed'). The 2023 review's own pooled estimate for the cohorts (1.18, or 1.24 in its text) is not mentioned.
findings.evidence: sc_leung_2023 key_findings[5] (use disorder 3.46; adjusted 2.80 single study), inclusion_exclusion (comparisons with other drug use excluded), reporting_issues[0] and [7] (drug class of Lin et al.), exposure.polysubstance ('speed'); evidence[4]; sc_mcketin_2019 key_findings[3] and [8].
findings.proposed: Use of methamphetamine or other amphetamines is associated with depressive symptoms in observational studies: pooled adjusted odds ratio 1.3 (95% CI 1.2–1.4; 6 studies, I² 0%; nearly all measuring symptoms) for any use in a 2019 review, and adjusted odds ratios of 1.60 and 1.50 in the two cohorts in its 2023 update that followed people over time while adjusting for earlier depressive symptoms (secondary-school students; men who have sex with men); that review's pooled estimate for these cohorts (1.18, or 1.24 in its text) cannot be reproduced from its tables. In unadjusted subgroups of the 2019 review, the association was present in general-population samples (2.0) but not within samples of people who use other substances (1.1, 0.7–1.7). For amphetamine use disorder the reviews differ: 1.2 (0.5–2.7; 6 studies, unadjusted) in the 2019 review, mostly against comparison groups that also used other drugs or had clinical conditions, and 3.46 (2.04–5.89; 2 cross-sectional studies, unadjusted) in the 2023 update, which excluded such comparisons. The 2023 review updates the 2019 one, with largely the same authors, so the two are not independent.

findings.rule: METHODS §6.3 overlapping evidence ('the claim says so'); GRADE domain logic
findings.issue: The two cited reviews overlap (the 2023 paper updates the 2019 review under the same PROSPERO protocol, with largely the same authors), but neither the reasoning nor the statement says so, as §6.3 requires. The reasoning also justifies no risk-of-bias downgrade by consistency (I² 0%), which is an inconsistency argument, and does not mention that neither review assessed publication bias (both AMSTAR 2 critically low).
findings.evidence: sc_leung_2023 design_detail (update of McKetin et al., 2019, same protocol), replication.where_it_stands, risk_of_bias (critically low; item 15 'no'); sc_mcketin_2019 risk_of_bias (item 15 'no').
findings.proposed: Certainty low and status 'replicated' kept. Reasoning: 'Observational, mostly cross-sectional; starts low. Rated for the association as worded. Risk of bias not downgraded: the headline estimates are adjusted (different covariate sets) and the two longitudinal cohorts adjusted for earlier depressive symptoms; residual confounding by other drug use and life circumstances is plausible (no association within substance-using samples) and is why the claim is worded as an association. Inconsistency not downgraded: adjusted any-use estimates agree (I² 0%) and the main heterogeneity is explained by sample type; the use-disorder estimates conflict between the reviews and are reported, not pooled. Indirectness not downgraded, but definitions range from mild screening thresholds (PHQ-9 of 5 or more) to diagnosed major depression, and methamphetamine is pooled with amphetamine. Publication bias was assessed in neither review. The 2023 review updates the 2019 one (same protocol, largely the same authors), so they are not independent; replicated rests on the independent primary studies within them (6 adjusted studies; two separate cohorts).'

findings.rule: brief check B
findings.issue: 'More likely to be depressed' overstates outcomes that were mostly symptom scales, some at mild thresholds. 'Among people who also use other drugs, the difference disappeared' misdescribes the comparison (people who use meth against other people who use drugs) and an unadjusted, imprecise estimate (1.1, 0.7–1.7). 'So other drug use and life circumstances may explain part of it' says more than the statement. The use-disorder disagreement is absent.
findings.evidence: evidence[1], [4]; sc_leung_2023 outcomes.validity_norms; statement.
findings.proposed: People who use meth or other amphetamines report depressive symptoms somewhat more often than people who don't: about 1.3 to 1.6 times the odds after accounting for some other factors, including in two studies that followed people over time. When people who use meth were compared with other people who use drugs, there was no clear difference. For people with a meth use disorder, the two main reviews disagree.

findings.rule: brief check F (claims that contradict each other)
findings.issue: 'Only one included study examined deaths by suicide' and the plain's 'Whether this means more deaths by suicide was examined in only one study' contradict cl_meth_mortality on the same page, which reports a pooled suicide standardized mortality ratio of 12.2 (4.89–30.47) and a crude suicide death rate of 0.20 per 100 person-years from cohorts of people with regular or problematic amphetamine use. The single study's own result is also left out.
findings.evidence: cl_meth_mortality magnitude; sc_stockings_2019 analysis.effect_sizes (suicide: 6 cohorts); sc_mcketin_2019 key_findings[7] (one completed-suicide study: deaths higher than expected but not significantly raised relative to opioid use); evidence[2].
findings.proposed: End the statement with: 'Only one study in this review examined deaths by suicide (in a drug-treatment follow-up, suicide deaths were higher than expected but not significantly higher than among people using opioids); a separate meta-analysis of cohorts of people with regular or problematic amphetamine use found suicide deaths about 12 times the rate of the general population of the same age and sex (see cl_meth_mortality).' Extend evidence[2].extracted accordingly. Plain: 'People with an amphetamine or meth use disorder are more likely to have suicidal thoughts and attempts: about 1.5 times the odds after accounting for some other factors. This review had little on deaths by suicide, but studies following people with regular or problematic use found suicide deaths about 12 times as common as in people of the same age and sex (see the mortality claim).'

findings.rule: brief check A (qualifying finding left out); METHODS §6.3 precision
findings.issue: The any-use estimate is given as 1.7 (1.0–2.9) without saying that its interval reaches no association, that I² is 77%, or that the paper's text gives 1.4 (the card says any claim should note this). The statement also omits how far adjustment reduced the estimates (use disorder 2.3 to 1.5; any use 4.4 to 1.7), which shows how strong the confounding is.
findings.evidence: sc_mcketin_2019 reporting_issues[0] (1.4 vs 1.7; note that the interval touches 1.0), key_findings[1] (any use unadjusted 4.4, 2.4–8.2), [4]; evidence[0], [1], [3].
findings.proposed: Amphetamine use disorder (amphetamine or methamphetamine) is associated with suicidal ideation and attempts: pooled adjusted odds ratio 1.5 (95% CI 1.3–1.8; 4 studies, I² 0%), down from 2.3 (1.8–2.9; 7 studies) unadjusted. For any use, adjustment reduced the estimate from 4.4 (2.4–8.2) to 1.7 (1.0–2.9; I² 77%; the review's text gives 1.4), an interval that reaches no association. [Then the ending proposed in the finding above.]

findings.rule: GRADE; METHODS §6.3 risk-of-bias rule; check C (reasoning matches domains)
findings.issue: The reasoning does not address risk of bias at all. The covariates behind the adjusted estimates are in an unread supplement, the unadjusted suicidality studies had among the lowest quality scores in the review (56–57%, as low as the violence studies, for which this page did downgrade), the large drop with adjustment shows strong confounding, and publication bias was not assessed.
findings.evidence: sc_mcketin_2019 outcomes.validity_norms (unadjusted suicidality 56–57%), analysis.covariates (supplement not read), risk_of_bias (critically low); cl_meth_violence grade.reasoning.
findings.proposed: Certainty low kept. Reasoning: 'Observational, mostly cross-sectional; starts low. Rated for the association as worded. Risk of bias not downgraded for the adjusted use-disorder estimate, which pooled 4 studies consistently (I² 0%, n=21,753), but the adjustment sets are unknown (unread supplement), the unadjusted suicidality studies had among the lowest quality scores (56–57%), and the drop from 2.3 to 1.5 with adjustment shows strong confounding, so residual confounding by depression and other psychiatric illness cannot be excluded; the claim is therefore worded as an association. The any-use estimate is imprecise and inconsistent (1.0–2.9; I² 77%) and is reported as such. Publication bias was not assessed (AMSTAR 2 critically low).'

findings.rule: brief check A; METHODS §6.3 (absence of evidence)
findings.issue: The violent-behaviour estimate (3.7) is an unadjusted post hoc subgroup, set beside the adjusted 1.4 without saying so; 'violent offending was not (OR 1.0)' turns an imprecise, heterogeneous estimate (0.4–2.7, I² 94%) into absence; and the bracketed list of measures has no anchor (the card lists self-reported acts, hostility scales and criminal records).
findings.evidence: sc_mcketin_2019 key_findings[6] (unadjusted subgroups), outcomes.instruments, analysis.preregistration_detail (post hoc); evidence[1].
findings.proposed: Whether amphetamine use (amphetamine or methamphetamine) is associated with violence after accounting for other factors is not established: the pooled adjusted odds ratio was 1.4 (95% CI 0.8–2.4; 6 studies), against 2.2 (1.2–4.1; 10 studies, I² 95%) unadjusted. In unadjusted post hoc subgroups, violent behaviour was associated (3.7, 3.1–4.5) and violent offending was not clearly associated (1.0, 0.4–2.7; I² 94%). The violence studies had among the lowest quality ratings in the review, with poor measurement of use.

findings.rule: METHODS §6.3 large effect; weakest necessary link
findings.issue: The large-effect upgrade is applied to a rise in death counts over calendar time. §6.3 applies it to an exposure-outcome estimate that stays large under the most adjusted model with no bias away from the null; a time trend has no such model, and calendar year is not an exposure whose effect is being estimated. The claim's other necessary parts (use +22%, use disorder +47%, with overlapping intervals between 2015 and 2019) are not large, so by the weakest-link rule the claim cannot be moderate on the strength of the death counts.
findings.evidence: Claim grade.reasoning; magnitude (intervals 1,394–1,829 vs 1,660–2,282; 578–905 vs 816–1,365); sc_han_2021 risk_of_bias (JBI moderate), validity_norms (T43.6; 85–90% of certificates mention methamphetamine).

Not upgraded: large effect concerns the size of an exposure's effect under adjustment, not a change in counts over time, and the claim's survey trends (+22% use, +47% use disorder; intervals overlapping between 2015 and 2019, trend tests significant) are not large. Risk of bias not downgraded for the trend (JBI moderate: the frame excludes unsheltered and institutionalized people and about half of sampled households completed an interview, which lowers the levels more than it changes the trend). The death series is a code (ICD-10 T43.6) of which 85–90% of certificates mention methamphetamine.'

The statement also omits that deaths without opioids also more than doubled (3,220 to 7,051), so the rise was not only in opioid co-involvement; that the death code covers psychostimulants other than cocaine; and that the survey excludes unsheltered and institutionalized people, so use is probably underestimated (an anchor already says so).

findings.rule: brief check B
findings.issue: The plain omits the age range, that the surveys miss people who are homeless or in institutions, that deaths without opioids also more than doubled, and that the data end in 2019 and later US figures use different methods; 'meth-type stimulants' would be clearer tied to the coding.
findings.evidence: Statement; evidence[4]; sc_han_2021 key_findings[1]; data/epidemiology/us.json.
findings.proposed: In US household surveys of adults aged 18 to 64, the estimated number who said they had used meth in the past year rose by about a fifth between 2015 and 2019, and the number with a meth use disorder by about half; the surveys miss people who are homeless or in institutions. Over the same years, overdose deaths involving stimulants other than cocaine (mostly meth) nearly tripled; more than half of the 2019 deaths also involved opioids, but deaths without opioids also more than doubled. The bigger percentages often quoted from this paper start from 2016, the lowest year. Later US figures use different methods and are not directly comparable.

findings.rule: brief check A (number vs anchor); METHODS §6.3 (relative effects with absolute effects where the base rate is known)
findings.issue: The statement attaches '25 cohorts' to the pooled estimates, but the all-cause crude rate and standardized ratio come from 23 cohorts (115,223 people) of the 25 included, as the anchors say. The cause-specific ratios are given without the cause-specific crude death rates the review reports, although §6.3 requires absolute effects beside relative ones. The statement also does not say that the ratios are standardized for age and sex only.
findings.evidence: evidence[0] (23 cohorts, 115,223 people), [1]; sc_stockings_2019 sample.n_by_group (25 cohorts; 23 in all-cause estimates), key_findings[3] (cause-specific crude rates), comparison.matching and unmeasured_premorbid.
findings.proposed: Statement: 'In 23 cohorts (115,223 people) of people with regular or problematic use of amphetamines (amphetamine or methamphetamine), mostly people in treatment, people who inject drugs, people with hospital diagnoses and people in contact with the criminal justice system, all-cause mortality was 1.11 deaths per 100 person-years (95% CI 0.90–1.37), 6.83 times (5.27–8.84) that of the general population of the same age and sex (5.71 in the 8 cohorts that reported their own ratios; ratios for 13 cohorts were imputed by the reviewers). In the 4 to 7 cohorts reporting each cause, crude death rates per 100 person-years were 0.20 for accidental injury, 0.20 for suicide, 0.14 for drug poisoning, 0.13 for cardiovascular disease and 0.03 for homicide; relative to the general population the excess was largest for drug poisoning (24.7 times), suicide (12.2) and homicide (11.9). Heterogeneity was very high (I² 97–98% for the all-cause estimates). The ratios are standardized for age and sex only, so they describe the excess mortality of these populations, which includes the effects of opioid and other drug use, injecting, infection, poverty and imprisonment, not the effect of amphetamines alone.' Magnitude, add: 'Cause-specific crude rates per 100 person-years: accidental injury 0.20 (0.08–0.47; 7 cohorts), suicide 0.20 (0.07–0.55; 6), drug poisoning 0.14 (0.06–0.34; 5), cardiovascular 0.13 (0.06–0.29; 4), homicide 0.03 (0.02–0.06; 4).' Add an anchor for Table 2's cause-specific crude rows.

findings.rule: brief check B (meaning changed)
findings.issue: 'Overdose, suicide, homicide, injuries and heart disease were the main causes' misreads ratios that rank causes by excess relative to the general population, not by how many people died: by crude rate, homicide was the least common of the five causes (0.03 per 100 person-years) and injuries and suicide the most common (0.20). The plain also leaves out the criminal-justice cohorts and that many in these cohorts also used opioids and other drugs.
findings.evidence: sc_stockings_2019 key_findings[3] (crude cause-specific rates), polysubstance (opioid and other drug use, not adjustable), sample.recruitment.
findings.proposed: In studies that followed people with regular or problematic use of amphetamines, including meth, about 1 in 90 died each year, nearly 7 times the rate of people of the same age and sex. Among the causes studied, injuries and suicide were the most common, followed by overdose and heart disease; compared with people of the same age and sex, overdose deaths were about 25 times as common, and suicide and homicide about 12 times. These were people in treatment, people who inject, people in hospital records or in contact with the justice system, not everyone who uses, and many also used opioids or other drugs, so not all of this excess is due to the stimulant.

findings.rule: METHODS §6.3 large effect ('no remaining bias runs away from the null'); GRADE
findings.issue: The large-effect upgrade breaks §6.3: the ratios are standardized for age and sex only, and the differences left unadjusted (opioid and other drug use, injecting, HIV and hepatitis C, homelessness, imprisonment) all run away from the null; the card states that the ratios measure the mortality of a disadvantaged population, not the effect of amphetamines. If the claim is read as descriptive, the upgrade's rationale does not apply; if as causal, its condition is not met. Removing only the upgrade gives very low; I propose also removing the inconsistency downgrade, because the heterogeneity concerns the size of the excess, not its presence.
findings.evidence: sc_stockings_2019 comparison.unmeasured_premorbid, cannot_establish, risk_of_bias.reasoning, key_findings[6] (regional ratios 4.48–10.52), [8] (5.71; 6.47 without the HIV cohort); evidence[4].
findings.proposed: large_effect 0; inconsistency 0; certainty 'low' (unchanged). Reasoning: 'Observational, starts low. Rated as a description of mortality in these cohorts relative to the general population, not as an effect of amphetamine use. Not upgraded for large effect: the ratios are standardized for age and sex only, and the differences left unadjusted (opioid and other drug use, injecting, infection, poverty, imprisonment) run away from the null (§6.3). Not downgraded for inconsistency: I² is 97–98%, but every regional point estimate (4.5–10.5) and both sensitivity analyses (5.71 in cohorts with their own ratios; 6.47 without the HIV cohort) show a several-fold excess, so the heterogeneity concerns the size of the excess, which is shown, not its presence. Not downgraded for indirectness because the claim is restricted to the populations sampled; older cohorts probably involved amphetamine more than crystalline methamphetamine. Risk of bias: cause-of-death ascertainment was often unclear and 13 of 23 ratios were imputed; not downgraded for the all-cause estimate.'

findings.rule: METHODS §8 section 10 (year-stamped); §10.1

findings.rule: brief check B; METHODS §9 (no adjectives of reassurance; certainty as rated)
findings.issue: 'Helped about 1 in 7 people' attributes every response on treatment to the medicines, although 2.5% responded on placebo; the treatment effect is 11 percentage points, about 1 extra responder per 9 treated. 'A real but modest effect' asserts a certainty the rating (moderate, one trial) does not carry. The plain drops that most people on treatment did not respond, that the response was measured in the last two weeks of each 6-week stage, that no outcome after treatment is reported, and that people using opioids were excluded. This plain is shown in the at-a-glance box.
findings.evidence: evidence[1]–[2]; sc_trivedi_2021 interpretation_gap.results_show (most participants did not respond), cannot_establish (no post-treatment outcome), inclusion_exclusion (opioid-free); site/src/app.views.js (at-a-glance renders plain).
findings.proposed: In one large US trial of adults who used meth almost every day, about 1 in 7 people given an injected medicine (naltrexone) plus a daily tablet (bupropion) had mostly meth-free urine tests in the last two weeks of a 6-week treatment period, compared with about 1 in 40 on placebo: about 1 extra person for every 9 treated. Most people on the medicines did not reach this, the trial did not report what happened after treatment ended, and people using opioids were not included. Nausea was common on the medicines.

findings.rule: METHODS §5.3 (domains behind any summary judgment); GRADE risk of bias
findings.issue: The reasoning gives one reason for not downgrading risk of bias, while the RoB 2 card has 'some concerns' in four of five domains: allocation concealment not described; blinding integrity not assessed with distinctive side effects; differential missing samples (the complete-case effect is 18.7 points); a weighted primary outcome that differs from the registry's stage-specific outcomes, and an unadjusted interim efficacy look. 'Conservative' should be explained: counting missing samples as non-response penalizes the arm with more missing samples, here the active arm.
findings.evidence: sc_trivedi_2021 risk_of_bias (domains and reasoning), sample.attrition (all four samples: 47.7% vs 60.2% in stage 1), key_findings[1], [2], [4], [8].
findings.proposed: Certainty moderate kept. Reasoning: 'Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled; starts high. Risk of bias (RoB 2 some concerns in randomization, deviations, missing data and selection of the reported result) not downgraded: the outcome is an objective urine result; missing samples were counted as non-response, which here penalizes the active arm, whose samples were more often missing (all four provided by 47.7% vs 60.2% in stage 1; the complete-case difference was 18.7 points); the registry's stage-specific outcomes are reported and each favours treatment (13.1 and 9.6 points, editors' calculation); functional unblinding is plausible (nausea 37.6% vs 15.3%) and could affect the size of the effect but would not plausibly create it. Imprecision −1: one trial with 31 responders on active treatment; the number needed to treat ranges from about 6 to 16. Indirectness not downgraded because the claim is restricted to the trial population (opioid-free, not in other treatment) and to the end-of-stage response.'

findings.rule: internal consistency (card vs claim); METHODS §6.3 editors' calculations
findings.issue: The card calls 6.3 a 'one-sided 95% lower boundary' and gives the two-sided interval as 6.2–16.0 from a rounded SE of 2.5, while the claim (after the second reader) treats 6.3 as the two-sided 95% lower limit with interval 6.3–15.9. From Wald z 4.53, SE is 2.45: a one-sided 95% bound would be about 7.1, so 6.3 is the one-sided 97.5% (two-sided 95%) lower limit, consistent with the trial's one-sided test at alpha 0.025. The claim is right; the card is not.
findings.evidence: Editors' arithmetic: 11.1/4.53 = 2.45; 11.1 − 1.645×2.45 = 7.07; 11.1 ± 1.96×2.45 = 6.30 to 15.90. sc_trivedi_2021 analysis.effect_sizes, outcomes (one-sided alpha 0.025); evidence[2]; claim changelog v0.2.2.
findings.proposed: Correct the card in all three places to: 'lower limit 6.3 (one-sided 97.5%, equal to the two-sided 95% lower limit); editors' two-sided 95% interval 6.3–15.9 from Wald z 4.53'; log the change in verification.editorial_corrections; confirm the printed wording at the source.

summary: The ten claims are carefully drafted, nearly all numbers match their anchors, and the language is mostly free of alarm or reassurance; many statements already carry the qualifiers a careful reader needs. Three problems recur in the claims. First, 'large effect' upgrades are applied where §6.3 does not allow them (the within-person psychosis cohort, the US trends, mortality), which lifts two claims to moderate and puts one into the at-a-glance box. Second, the psychosis-course and psychosis-versus-schizophrenia claims rest only on narrative reviews, contrary to §5.3 and to their own cards, while a 2019 systematic review and a 2024 meta-analysis on these questions sit unread on the reading list. Third, three plain texts change the meaning (a treatment 'helped 1 in 7'; causes ranked by relative excess called 'main causes'; a 'lasting' psychotic illness), which matters more because the at-a-glance box shows plain text; and the depression and suicidality claims report selectively or contradict the mortality claim. At page level the picture is non-alarmist but leans toward reassurance by omission: physical harms, the base rate of psychosis and the treatment evidence beyond one trial are absent without a note, the systematic search is incomplete, and the at-a-glance picks do not follow the ratings.
